claim: Stop codon readthrough is essential to diverse viruses.
source: Stop codon readthrough, the decoding of a stop codon as a sense codon by the ribosome, plays important regulatory roles. Most immediately, readthrough diversifies the proteome by creating a pool of C-terminally extended proteins. In this capacity, it is essential to a variety of plant and animal viruses (Cimino et al., 2011; Li and Rice, 1989; Napthine et al., 2012; Skuzeski et al., 1991; Yoshinaka et al., 1985; reviewed in Beier and Grimm, 2001; Firth and Brierley, 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies showing readthrough is essential to viruses

claim: Readthrough diversifies the proteome by creating C-terminally extended proteins.
source: Most immediately, readthrough diversifies the proteome by creating a pool of C-terminally extended proteins.
evidence: The introduction states this as an established fact

claim: Readthrough can suppress pathological phenotypes caused by premature stop codons.
source: In eukaryotic host genes, readthrough is functionally important insofar as it may suppress pathological phenotypes caused by premature stop codons (Kopczynski et al., 1992; Fearon et al., 1994)
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing this function

claim: Readthrough can antagonize nonsense-mediated decay.
source: In eukaryotic host genes, readthrough is functionally important insofar as it may suppress pathological phenotypes caused by premature stop codons (Kopczynski et al., 1992; Fearon et al., 1994), antagonize nonsense-mediated decay (Keeling et al., 2004)
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing this function

claim: Readthrough can modulate protein activity by changing C-terminal sequence.
source: by changing the C-terminal sequence of a given protein, modulate its activity (Torabi and Kruglyak, 2012)
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing this function

claim: Readthrough can modulate protein stability by changing C-terminal sequence.
source: by changing the C-terminal sequence of a given protein, modulate its activity (Torabi and Kruglyak, 2012), stability (Namy et al., 2002)
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing this function

claim: Readthrough can modulate protein localization by changing C-terminal sequence.
source: by changing the C-terminal sequence of a given protein, modulate its activity (Torabi and Kruglyak, 2012), stability (Namy et al., 2002), and/or localization (Freitag et al., 2012)
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing this function

claim: In yeast, translation termination efficiency is modulated by [PSI+], an epigenetic state resulting from prion-like aggregates of Sup35p.
source: In yeast, the efficiency of translation termination is modulated by [PSI+], an epigenetic state resulting from prion-like aggregates of Sup35p, the yeast homologue of the translation termination factor eRF3 (reviewed in Tuite and Cox, 2007).
evidence: The introduction cites a review describing this phenomenon

claim: Various yeast strains exhibit [PSI+]-dependent fitness advantages.
source: Various yeast strains exhibit [PSI+]-dependent fitness advantages, implying that increased readthrough activates useful genetic diversity that is ordinarily masked by stop codons (True and Lindquist, 2000; Halfmann et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing this finding

claim: A baseline level of readthrough appears beneficial in wild [psi−] yeast strains.
source: In addition, a small baseline level of readthrough appears to be beneficial in wild [psi−] yeast strains, as alleles of various factors controlling termination efficiency are under balancing selection (Torabi and Kruglyak, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing this finding

claim: Only a handful of eukaryotic host genes have been experimentally demonstrated to undergo readthrough in wild-type or prion-free organisms.
source: To date, only a handful of eukaryotic host genes have been experimentally demonstrated to undergo readthrough in wild-type or prion-free organisms (Geller and Rich, 1980; Xue and Cooley, 1993; Klagges et al., 1996; Steneberg et al., 1998; Namy et al., 2002; Jungreis et al., 2011; Freitag et al., 2012; Torabi and Kruglyak, 2012; Yamaguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites all known examples at the time

claim: 283 readthrough events were predicted in Drosophila melanogaster using phylogenetic algorithms.
source: Using this approach, 283 readthrough events were predicted in Drosophila melanogaster, six of which they confirmed experimentally (Lin et al., 2007; Jungreis et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites the phylogenetic prediction studies

claim: Phylogenetic algorithms are limited in their ability to detect evolutionarily recent readthrough events.
source: While these algorithms provide a powerful means to identify ancient and phylogenetically conserved readthrough events, they are limited in their ability to detect evolutionarily recent events.
evidence: The introduction states this limitation of phylogenetic approaches

claim: Bioinformatic approaches cannot identify the tissues or cell types in which readthrough occurs.
source: Nor can bioinformatic approaches identify a priori the tissues or cell types in which readthrough occurs, measure the fraction of ribosomes that read through a given stop codon, or determine whether any of these processes are regulated: such questions demand experimental approaches.
evidence: The introduction states this limitation of bioinformatic approaches

claim: Drosophila ribosomes are highly sensitive to RNase I.

evidence: The results section describes this finding with reference to a figure and citations

claim: Drosophila ribosomes tolerate micrococcal nuclease (MNase) over a wide range of concentrations.

claim: Strong correlation (r2 = 0.998) was observed between technical replicates for genes with at least 128 reads.

evidence: The results section reports this correlation coefficient with reference to a figure
